paras: The Monessen saloon riot was a fight between white and Black coal miners in a saloon at Monessen, Pennsylvania, late on the night of September 7, 1903, in which a white miner, Lemuel Gilmore, was fatally shot. George Williams, a Black miner reported as the shooter, escaped with another Black man, William Griffey, and a crowd of white miners pursued them intending to lynch Williams. The pursuers did not catch him, and a Pittsburg dispatch about the "race riot" ran in papers from Georgia to Kansas.

According to a Pittsburg dispatch, the riot broke out late at night in a Monessen saloon "between white and colored coal miners." During the fighting Gilmore, who was white, was fatally shot, and the dispatch named Williams, described as "colored" or "a negro," as the man who fired. None of the versions says how the riot began or how many men took part.

Williams and Griffey escaped from the saloon. The fullest version of the dispatch said they were "being pursued by a crowd of white miners, with the avowed intention of lynching Williams if captured." No officers are mentioned in any of the reports.

No report of Williams's capture, an arrest, an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage. A paragraph in the Montgomery Advertiser on September 13, naming neither town nor man, said that Pennsylvanians "who wanted to lynch a negro" had not been able to catch him.

The story reached readers mainly as a short wire item from Pittsburg. The Savannah Morning News printed the fullest version on September 8 under the headline "MINERS IN A FIGHT" and the deck "White Man Was Fatally Shot by a Negro Miner," the only version to name Griffey or mention the lynching pursuit. The Bee of Earlington, Kentucky, headed it "Killed In a Race Riot" on September 10 and closed with "The murderer escaped." A still shorter version, "Race Riot in a Saloon," ran on September 11 and 12 in the Barton County Democrat and the Kinsley Graphic in Kansas and the Laclede Blade in Missouri, ending with the shooting.

In these trimmed versions the threat to lynch Williams dropped out, leaving a killing of a white man by a Black man. The one comment on the pursuit came from the South: the Montgomery Advertiser called it "a grievous disappointment" to the would-be lynchers and said they "did their best but failed to have their fun." No Black-press coverage and no report from a Pennsylvania paper was found.

reader.title: Monessen saloon riot
bases: The anti-Black violence reported is an attempted lynching: after the saloon shooting a crowd of white miners pursued George Williams 'with the avowed intention of lynching' him (A1), and an editorial said they 'couldn't catch him' (A6); no one was reported harmed by the crowd.

The saloon shooting appears in three versions of one Pittsburg wire dispatch (A1, A2, A3), but the pursuit and lynching intent appear only in A1, with A6 an unnamed editorial allusion; no local or independent report was found.

accounts.gist: During a late-night riot in a Monessen saloon between white and Black coal miners, Williams fatally shot Gilmore; Williams and Griffey escaped and were pursued by white miners intent on lynching Williams.

accounts.label: Pittsburg wire report (abridged)
accounts.gist: A 'race riot' in a Monessen saloon in which Williams fatally shot Gilmore; one version adds only that 'The murderer escaped'.

accounts.label: Southern editorial
accounts.gist: Pennsylvanians who wanted to lynch a Black man 'couldn't catch him' and 'failed to have their fun'.

framing.detail: Brief Pittsburg dispatch headed 'MINERS IN A FIGHT', 'Killed In a Race Riot' or 'Race Riot in a Saloon', reporting the lynching intent without comment and calling Williams 'The murderer'.
The Montgomery Advertiser used the failed pursuit to needle Northern lynchers, calling it a 'grievous disappointment' that they 'failed to have their fun'.
